name: GERD / non-cardiac chest pain

matching.reasoningTemplate: Chest pain without ischaemic features or risk factors may be oesophageal, but cardiac causes must be excluded first.

redFlags: Do not attribute to GERD until ACS excluded

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e: Chest Discomfort ch.15 p.104-109; Diseases of the Esophagus ch.334 p.2503-2511; Nausea, Vomiting, and Indigestion ch.48 p.300-301
clinicalPearls: Esophageal pain shares a nerve plexus with the heart and esophageal afferents discriminate stimuli poorly, so distention or acid (chemostimulation) is often perceived as pressure-type mid-chest pain radiating to back, arms, or jaw - closely mimicking angina (p.2503-2504).

Features that favour an oesophageal rather than cardiac source include pain that is nonexertional, prolonged, meal-related, relieved by antacids, accompanied by heartburn/dysphagia/regurgitation, and that interrupts sleep - but every one of these overlaps with cardiac pain, which must remain the primary consideration (p.2509).

Heartburn (pyrosis) is the most common oesophageal symptom and its link to GERD is strong enough that empirical acid-suppression has become accepted management; chest pain and persistent dysphagia are the key exceptions that warrant evaluation rather than empirical treatment (p.2503, p.2510).
Gastrointestinal disorders are the single most common cause of nontraumatic chest discomfort, yet fewer than 15% of ED chest-pain presentations turn out to be ACS (p.104).

A burning quality suggests acid reflux but can also occur with myocardial ischaemia; conversely oesophageal spasm can produce a severe squeezing pain identical to angina - quality alone never establishes a diagnosis (p.105).

Both reflux relief and ischaemia relief overlap with nitroglycerin: oesophageal spasm may be relieved promptly by nitroglycerin just as angina can be, so a nitroglycerin response does not confirm cardiac origin (p.106).
Chest wall tenderness on palpation does NOT exclude myocardial ischaemia, and a normal physical exam is not reassuring in unstable ischaemic heart disease (p.106-107).
Some patients with acid reflux on pH testing report epigastric/abdominal pain or nausea instead of classic heartburn (atypical GERD) (p.301, ch.48).
Visceral hypersensitivity is increasingly recognised as a cofactor in GERD symptom generation, beyond simple mucosal erosion and afferent nerve activation (p.2510).
harrison.pathophysiology: Pathologic reflux arises from anatomic and physiologic failure of the oesophagogastric junction valve - widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus with diminished crural diaphragm function, loss of the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment disabling the flap valve, axial (sliding) hiatus hernia causing LES hypotension, and increased junctional compliance allowing liquid to escape during transient LES relaxations (the belch reflex). Some reflux is physiologic and intertwined with belching, but esophagitis follows excessive reflux plus impaired acid clearance, which depends on peristalsis returning fluid to the stomach and bicarbonate in swallowed saliva neutralising residual acid; impaired peristalsis and reduced salivation therefore prolong acid contact. Mucosal injury is driven by a cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway rather than purely direct caustic injury. Gastric acid hypersecretion is usually NOT the dominant factor (exceptions: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe esophagitis in ~50%); chronic H. pylori gastritis may even be protective by inducing hypoacidity. Pepsin, bile, and pancreatic enzymes also injure the epithelium, and bile persists in refluxate despite acid suppression and is implicated as a cofactor in Barrett's metaplasia and adenocarcinoma. Exacerbating factors include abdominal obesity, pregnancy, gastric hypersecretory states, delayed gastric emptying, disrupted peristalsis, and overeating. Esophageal chest pain itself reflects a shared nerve plexus with the heart and poor discriminative ability of oesophageal afferents (p.2503-2504, p.2509-2510).
additionalDifferentials: Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial ischaemia (must be excluded first given lethal implications)
Distal (diffuse) esophageal spasm - dysphagia plus chest pain from abnormal contractions with normal LES relaxation; diagnosed only after commoner causes excluded
Peptic ulcer disease (symptomatic 60-90 min after meals)
Functional dyspepsia (postprandial distress and epigastric pain syndromes)
Pericarditis (radiation to trapezius ridge, worse supine, relieved leaning forward)
Costochondritis / Tietze's syndrome and other musculoskeletal chest-wall causes
Panic disorder / anxiety state (up to ~10% of ED chest-pain presentations)
Esophageal rupture (greatest urgency among noncardiopulmonary causes)
infectionMimics: Infectious esophagitis (fungal or viral) - more often causes odynophagia than heartburn; ulcerations are numerous, punctate, and diffuse on endoscopy
Pneumonia / pleuritis (pulmonary infective cause of chest pain via pleural involvement)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pill (medication-induced) esophagitis - solitary deep ulcer at points of luminal narrowing, often near the carina, sparing distal esophagus
Eosinophilic esophagitis - edema, rings, linear furrows, white punctate exudate, strictures
Distal esophageal spasm and hypercontractile esophagus
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG within 10 min of presentation, with serial ECGs every 30-60 min when ACS suspected; note resting ECG sensitivity for ischaemia is poor (as low as 20%)

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin at presentation and repeated (1-3 h hs-assay; 3-6 h conventional) - a rising/falling pattern with a value above the 99th percentile defines MI; a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after onset can rule out MI with NPV >99%
Validated clinical decision pathways (e.g., HEART, EDACS) combined with serial troponin to risk-stratify and safely discharge low-probability ACS patients

Coronary CT angiography or functional stress imaging (nuclear perfusion / stress echo) for intermediate/undetermined risk once life-threatening causes excluded; CTA can also exclude dissection, effusion, and PE
Chest radiograph (mediastinal widening, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pulmonary edema)
D-dimer to help exclude pulmonary embolism where indicated

Upper endoscopy (EGD) - first-line for mucosal lesions, Barrett's detection by color, biopsy of suspicious or atypical findings; erosive esophagitis is found in only ~one-third of GERD patients so a normal EGD does NOT exclude GERD
Ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring (24 h, or wireless capsule 48-96 h off acid suppression) - the diagnostic standard for confirming pathologic reflux
Combined esophageal pH-impedance testing (on PPI) to identify oesophageal hypersensitivity or nonacid/incompletely controlled acid regurgitation in refractory/atypical symptoms
High-resolution esophageal manometry (with FLIP/impedance) - to diagnose motility disorders (achalasia, DES) and assess peristalsis before anti-reflux surgery
Barium contrast radiography - higher sensitivity than endoscopy for strictures (especially with a 13-mm barium tablet) and for assessing function/anatomy
redFlags: Dysphagia (concerning for oesophageal obstruction - stricture, EoE, or cancer)
Odynophagia (suggests infectious or pill esophagitis, or extensive ulceration)
Occult or gross gastrointestinal bleeding / anaemia
Heartburn >5 years' duration, especially age >50, or new dyspepsia age >60 (screen for Barrett's / malignancy by endoscopy)
Failure to respond to acid suppression (up to one-third of presumed GERD)
Any diagnostic doubt about a cardiac cause - acute exertional/pressure pain, radiation to both arms, diaphoresis, dyspnoea, syncope, hypotension/tachycardia
harrison.prognosis: Most patients in whom an acute cardiopulmonary cause is excluded have a favourable prognosis; in low-risk patients the 30-day major cardiovascular event rate is about 2.5%. However, historically 2-6% of presumed-nonischaemic chest pain patients discharged from the ED were later found to have had a missed myocardial infarction, underscoring the cost of misclassification. For GERD itself, erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become rare with potent acid suppression, but Barrett's metaplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma have increased; progression of Barrett's to adenocarcinoma is estimated at roughly 0.1-0.5% per year, with obese white men in their sixth decade at greatest risk. High-grade dysplasia in Barrett's carries a high rate of progression and a high prevalence of coexisting unrecognised cancer (p.104, p.2510-2511, ch.85 p.92).
pitfalls: Attributing chest pain to GERD before excluding a cardiac cause - coronary artery disease must be given early consideration because of its potentially lethal implications, and oesophageal pain closely mimics angina.

Relying on pain quality, nitroglycerin response, or chest-wall tenderness to distinguish cardiac from oesophageal pain - all overlap and none is reliable; a normal exam and even a normal resting ECG do not exclude ischaemia.
Treating a normal endoscopy as ruling out GERD - erosive esophagitis is seen in only about one-third of GERD patients.
Overlooking that up to one-third of presumed-GERD patients fail to respond to acid suppression and may have an alternative diagnosis (functional, hypersensitivity, motility, nonacid reflux).

Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm or nonspecific manometric abnormalities prematurely - these are made only after GERD, peptic and infectious esophagitis, and cardiac disease are excluded; minor manometric findings are of unclear significance and often coexist with anxiety/depression and IBS.
Missing alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding/anaemia) that mandate endoscopy rather than continued empirical therapy.
Forgetting that nausea/vomiting and epigastric pain can accompany MI (especially inferior MI via vagal/Bezold-Jarisch reflex) and need not indicate a GI cause.
harrison.severityClassification: GERD spans a spectrum of oesophageal injury: nonerosive reflux disease, erosive esophagitis (graded by antisecretory-responsive severity), peptic stricture, Barrett's metaplasia, and adenocarcinoma. Barrett's dysplasia is staged as low-grade vs high-grade, the latter mandating intervention. For the chest-pain presentation itself, Harrison frames risk by clinical decision pathways categorising patients as low, intermediate, or high probability of ACS using symptoms, age, risk factors, ECG, and serial high-sensitivity troponin (HEART/EDACS scores) (p.107-109, p.2510-2511).
